VIDEO.title: The Most Unfair Parable Jesus Ever Told
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

kicker: Study aid · Matthew 20:1-16 · Episode 39 (#42 of 58 in the playlist)
hand: Or is your eye envious because I am generous?
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 20:1-16. A landowner hires laborers for his vineyard early in the morning for a denarius, then more at the third, sixth, ninth and eleventh hours, promising 'whatever is right.' At evening he pays the last first, a denarius each. Those hired first expect more, receive a denarius, and grumble: 'you have made them equal to us.' He answers that he did them no wrong: is it not lawful for him to do what he wishes with his own, or is their eye envious because he is generous? So the last shall be first, and the first last.

The parable continues Jesus' answer to Peter (19:27-30), and 'the last … first' frames it on both sides. The video follows Craig Blomberg in seeing 19:1-20:16 as one unit, bookended by two questions: 'Is it lawful?' (19:3) and 'Is it not lawful?' (20:15).

A vineyard would make any Jew think of Israel. A denarius was a normal day's wage, and the Torah required day laborers to be paid before sunset (Deuteronomy 24:15; Leviticus 19:13). The lesson lies in the surprise: the master lines everyone up to be paid, last first, so all can see.

The first workers were not cheated; they complain because the master 'made them equal.' Their grumbling recalls Israel in the wilderness (Numbers 14:27). 'Is your eye envious' is literally 'is your eye evil,' the Hebrew idiom ayin ra'ah for stinginess (Proverbs 23:6; 28:22; Matthew 6:23). Vinedressers, wealth and a double portion in Isaiah 61 suggest the logic of Jubilee.
The lesson: the real currency in the kingdom of heaven is not money, it's mercy. Those fit for the kingdom must have God's good eye and extend radical mercy to all who need it.
QUOTES: The real currency in the kingdom of heaven is not money, it's mercy.
Those who are fit for the kingdom of heaven must have God's good eye.
People ultimately find what they're looking for.
Peter says he left everything. What is he receiving in return? Everything.

method.p: Jesus' parables are meant to surprise and shock, so the lesson usually sits in the surprising moments. Here: the master keeps hiring, pays the last first in front of everyone, and gives them a full day's wage.

LSB_QUOTES.text: For the kingdom of heaven is like a landowner who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard.
Is it not lawful for me to do what I wish with what is my own? Or is your eye envious because I am generous?’

VINEYARD.title: Is it lawful? Is it not lawful?

left.text: And some Pharisees came to Jesus, testing Him and saying, “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any reason at all?”

right.text: Is it not lawful for me to do what I wish with what is my own? Or is your eye envious because I am generous?’

lines.text: The video follows Craig Blomberg: three controversial stories (marriage, the rich ruler, the vineyard) form one thematic unit, framed by two questions. Pay attention to bookends; there is greater depth to discover.
The LSB keeps the echo: both verses use the Greek exestin, 'it is lawful.'

left.text: “For the kingdom of heaven is like a landowner who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard.

right.text: For the vineyard of Yahweh of hosts is the house of Israel / And the men of Judah His delightful plant. / Thus He hoped for justice, but behold, bloodshed; / For righteousness, but behold, a cry of distress.

lines.text: The moment a Jew heard 'vineyard' he should have thought of Israel, the way God and His prophets sometimes characterized His people. So who stands in for the master of the house?

src.text: And about the eleventh hour he went out and found others standing around; and he *said to them, ‘Why have you been standing here idle all day long?’ They *said to him, ‘Because no one hired us.’ He *said to them, ‘You go into the vineyard too.’

lines.text: A denarius was the normal pay for a full day. Counting from about 6 a.m., the master goes out again at the third hour (9 a.m.), sixth (noon), ninth (3 p.m.) and eleventh (5 p.m.).
Why so many trips? We're not told. Perhaps it helps to know that day laborers who were not hired, and their families, would probably go hungry that night.
Only the first group is promised a denarius; the rest are told 'whatever is right I will give you' (20:4).

left.text: “Now when evening came, the owner of the vineyard *said to his foreman, ‘Call the laborers and pay them their wages, beginning with the last group to the first.’

right.text: You shall give him his wages on his day before the sun goes down, for he is afflicted and sets his soul on it, so that he will not cry against you to Yahweh and it become sin in you.

lines.text: Leviticus 19:13 says the same: a hired worker is paid at the end of each day. Paying the last first means everyone had to line up and watch; the master seems to do it on purpose.
The Mishnah: 'A day laborer collects his wages from his employer all night following his work shift' (Mishnah Bava Metzia 9:11).

EYE.title: You have made them equal to us

src.text: saying, ‘These last men have worked only one hour, and you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat.’ But he answered and said to one of them, ‘Friend, I am doing you no wrong; did you not agree with me for a denarius?

lines.text: Only the first workers complain. They were not treated improperly: they agreed to a denarius and received exactly what they were promised. No harm, no foul.
Their problem is that the master made the others equal to them. Now we're on to something.

left.text: Now when they received it, they were grumbling at the landowner,

right.text: “How long shall I bear with this evil congregation who are grumbling against Me? I have heard the complaints of the sons of Israel, which they are making against Me.

lines.text: Their grumbling recalls Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 16:7-12; Numbers 14:27; Deuteronomy 1:27). The circumstances differ, but the spirit of discontentment is the same: God provides, and they still complain.

left.text: Is it not lawful for me to do what I wish with what is my own? Or is your eye envious because I am generous?’

right.text: A man with an evil eye hurries after wealth / And does not know that want will come upon him.

lines.text: The last phrase is literally 'Is your eye evil because I am good?' A bad eye, ayin ra'ah, is a Hebrew idiom for being stingy and miserly. Proverbs 23:6 uses it too: the LSB's 'selfish man' is literally 'evil of eye.'
Someone with a bad eye looks for what is bad in the world and in other people, hence grumbling. People ultimately find what they're looking for, and miss what God is doing.

src.text: “The eye is the lamp of the body; so then if your eye is clear, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is bad, your whole body will be full of darkness. If then the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!

lines.text: Jesus repeats the concept from the Sermon on the Mount. The master has God's good eye; the 6 a.m. workers do not, because their complaint is about his generosity to others, not his treatment of them.

left.text: The Spirit of Lord Yahweh is upon me / Because Yahweh has anointed me / To bring good news to the afflicted; / He has sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, / To proclaim release to captives / And freedom to prisoners,

right.text: You shall thus set apart as holy the fiftieth year and proclaim a release through the land to all its inhabitants. It shall be a jubilee for you, and each of you shall return to his own possession of land, and each of you shall return to his family.

lines.text: Where does Jesus draw these stories from? The video points to Isaiah 61, the year of the Lord's favor, and the year of Jubilee.
Jesus read Isaiah 61:1-2 in the Nazareth synagogue: 'To proclaim the favorable year of the Lord' (Luke 4:19).

src.text: Strangers will stand and pasture your flocks, / And foreigners will be your farmers and your vinedressers. / But you will be called the priests of Yahweh; / You will be spoken of as ministers of our God. / You will eat the wealth of nations, / And in their glories you will boast. / Instead of your shame you will have a double portion, / And instead of dishonor they will shout for joy over their portion. / Therefore they will possess a double portion in their land; / Everlasting gladness will be theirs.

lines.text: A vineyard, vinedressers, wealth, a portion of payment, a double portion: the parable illustrates the logic of Jubilee. There is some kind of Jubilee theology the story is drawing from.
In Isaiah the foreigners work Israel's fields while Israel serves as priests; the link to the parable's laborers is the video's reading.

MERCY.title: What then will there be for us?

src.text: Then Peter answered and said to Him, “Behold, we have left everything and followed You; what then will there be for us?”

lines.text: The disciples shared something of the rich ruler's mindset that people earn God's favor. Peter left everything; what does he receive? Everything: relationship with God and eternal life.
The kingdom cannot be understood with a business mentality of wages earned. It trades on God's grace and mercy, extended to whomever He pleases.

Jesus tells of a master who seems to throw his wealth away, because the real currency in the parable is not money but mercy. To be rich in God's kingdom has everything to do with being close to the Lord.
The unit began with man's bad eye and ends with God's good eye. Marriage and wealth alike have an outward arrow: vehicles to extend God's blessing to others, so everyone is blessed.
Put on the glasses of radical generosity and you will see potential, providence and opportunities to spread the kingdom.

TERMS.def: A literary bookend: matching words at the start and end that frame a unit (19:3; 20:15).
A Roman silver coin, the normal pay for a full day's work.
Counted from sunrise: third hour about 9 a.m., sixth noon, ninth 3 p.m., eleventh 5 p.m.
Hebrew 'evil eye': stinginess, a begrudging spirit.
The fiftieth year of release, when land returned and slaves went free (Leviticus 25).
A story that surprises; the lesson is often in the surprising moment.

WORDS.gloss: To grumble, mutter. Look up: BDAG, γογγύζω.
Evil, bad. Look up: BDB or HALOT, רע.
Ram's horn; the year of jubilee.

BACKGROUND.p: Day laborers gathered in the marketplace to be hired (20:3) and lived hand to mouth. The Torah protected them: wages before sunset (Deuteronomy 24:15). On working hours the Mishnah says everything follows 'the regional custom in these matters' (Mishnah Bava Metzia 7:1).
Harvest and pruning needed many hands at once, which helps explain repeated hiring. Vineyards had walls and watchtowers (Isaiah 5:2), and the vineyard was a standing picture of Israel.

Every fiftieth year land returned to its families and Israelite slaves were released (Leviticus 25:8-17). Isaiah 61 takes up the language of release for the coming age, and Jesus reads it at Nazareth (Luke 4:18-21).

DEBATES.h: Who are the first and the last?
DEBATES.p: Readings include Israel and the Gentiles, the disciples and later believers, the religious leaders and sinners, and those converted early or late in life (Chrysostom's view). The video applies it to anyone with a wage-earning mindset.

DEBATES.h: Is the parable about salvation or rewards?
DEBATES.p: Some see one gift of eternal life for all; others see a warning about comparing rewards. Both read the denarius as grace, not pay.
The video hears Isaiah 61 and Jubilee in the parable. Others see the main background in Israel as God's vineyard (Isaiah 5) and in Torah laws on wages.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: A denarius was a Roman coin; a drachma was a Greek coin of roughly the same value, not another name for it.
The 10-hour workday attributed to D. A. Carson is given without a source; the Mishnah says working hours follow local custom (Bava Metzia 7:1).
The Craig Blomberg passage on the inclusio is read from a commentary the video does not name, so this page summarizes it rather than quoting it.
In 20:15 the LSB already has 'Is it not lawful' and 'is your eye envious,' where the video's translation reads am I not allowed and do you begrudge my generosity.
Proverbs 23:6 reads 'a selfish man' in the LSB and 28:22 'a man with an evil eye'; the video's translation says stingy for both.

QUESTIONS: Which worker do you identify with first, and why?
Why does the master pay the last first, in front of everyone?
What is the difference between being treated unfairly and being treated generously to someone else?
Where do you notice a 'bad eye' in yourself, looking for what is wrong?
How do marriage and wealth point outward, as vehicles of blessing?
Whom could you extend 'radical mercy' to this week?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The lesson, stated plainly: the real currency in the kingdom of heaven is not money, it's mercy. Those who are fit for the kingdom must have God's good eye and extend radical mercy to all who need it. In God's kingdom, true satisfaction comes from seeing everyone blessed, not just yourself. If God's people truly understood this, no one would ask whether divorce is allowed or how many deeds earn entrance. Marriage and wealth are vehicles to extend God's blessings to others. The world's influence comes in like the tide; we can't think like the world. Put on the glasses of radical generosity and you will see potential, providence and opportunities to spread the kingdom.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): the next time you hear of someone else's blessing, notice your first reaction. Thank God for it out loud, and pray Matthew 6:22 for a clear eye.

   (video) Their grumbling recalls Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 16:7-12; Numbers 14:27; Deuteronomy 1:27). The circumstances differ, but the spirit of discontentment is the same: God provides, and they still complain. (Exodus 16:7; Deuteronomy 1:27)
3. Matthew 20:15; Proverbs 28:22: Is your eye evil?
   The landowner (Matthew 20:15, LSB): "Is it not lawful for me to do what I wish with what is my own? Or is your eye envious because I am generous?’"
   Proverbs (Proverbs 28:22, LSB): "A man with an evil eye hurries after wealth / And does not know that want will come upon him."
   (video) The last phrase is literally 'Is your eye evil because I am good?' A bad eye, ayin ra'ah, is a Hebrew idiom for being stingy and miserly. Proverbs 23:6 uses it too: the LSB's 'selfish man' is literally 'evil of eye.' (Proverbs 23:6)
   (video) Someone with a bad eye looks for what is bad in the world and in other people, hence grumbling. People ultimately find what they're looking for, and miss what God is doing.
4. Matthew 6:22-23: The lamp of the body
   Said before Matthew 6:22-23: "“The eye is the lamp of the body; so then if your eye is clear, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is bad, your whole body will be full of darkness. If then the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+6:22-23
   (video) Jesus repeats the concept from the Sermon on the Mount. The master has God's good eye; the 6 a.m. workers do not, because their complaint is about his generosity to others, not his treatment of them.

## Not money, but mercy
1. Isaiah 61:1-2; Leviticus 25:10: The favorable year
   Isaiah (Isaiah 61:1, LSB): "The Spirit of Lord Yahweh is upon me / Because Yahweh has anointed me / To bring good news to the afflicted; / He has sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, / To proclaim release to captives / And freedom to prisoners,"
   Torah (Leviticus 25:10, LSB): "You shall thus set apart as holy the fiftieth year and proclaim a release through the land to all its inhabitants. It shall be a jubilee for you, and each of you shall return to his own possession of land, and each of you shall return to his family."
   (video) Where does Jesus draw these stories from? The video points to Isaiah 61, the year of the Lord's favor, and the year of Jubilee.
   [Background] Jesus read Isaiah 61:1-2 in the Nazareth synagogue: 'To proclaim the favorable year of the Lord' (Luke 4:19). (Luke 4:19)
2. Isaiah 61:5-7: Vinedressers and a double portion
   Remez Isaiah 61:5-7: "Strangers will stand and pasture your flocks, / And foreigners will be your farmers and your vinedressers. / But you will be called the priests of Yahweh; / You will be spoken of as ministers of our God. / You will eat the wealth of nations, / And in their glories you will boast. / Instead of your shame you will have a double portion, / And instead of dishonor they will shout for joy over their portion. / Therefore they will possess a double portion in their land; / Everlasting gladness will be theirs." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Isaiah+61:5-7
   (video) A vineyard, vinedressers, wealth, a portion of payment, a double portion: the parable illustrates the logic of Jubilee. There is some kind of Jubilee theology the story is drawing from.
   [Background] In Isaiah the foreigners work Israel's fields while Israel serves as priests; the link to the parable's laborers is the video's reading.
3. Matthew 19:27: What then will there be for us?
   Everything Matthew 19:27: "Then Peter answered and said to Him, “Behold, we have left everything and followed You; what then will there be for us?”" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+19:27
   (video) The disciples shared something of the rich ruler's mindset that people earn God's favor. Peter left everything; what does he receive? Everything: relationship with God and eternal life.
   (video) The kingdom cannot be understood with a business mentality of wages earned. It trades on God's grace and mercy, extended to whomever He pleases.
4. The lesson: Not money, but mercy
   (video) Jesus tells of a master who seems to throw his wealth away, because the real currency in the parable is not money but mercy. To be rich in God's kingdom has everything to do with being close to the Lord.
   (video) The unit began with man's bad eye and ends with God's good eye. Marriage and wealth alike have an outward arrow: vehicles to extend God's blessing to others, so everyone is blessed.
   (video) Put on the glasses of radical generosity and you will see potential, providence and opportunities to spread the kingdom.

## Key people
- The landowner: Hires all day, pays everyone a denarius, and has God's good eye. [Background] In Isaiah 5 the vineyard's owner is Yahweh Himself.
- The first laborers: Hired at about 6 a.m.; paid what they agreed, they grumble at the master's generosity. [Background] Compare the older brother in Luke 15:28-30.
- The eleventh-hour laborers: Hired at about 5 p.m. because no one hired them; paid a full denarius. [Background] 'The last shall be first' (20:16).
- The foreman: Pays the workers, last first, so all can see. [Background] Greek epitropos, a steward or manager (20:8).
- Simon Peter: His question, 'what then will there be for us?', sets up the parable. [Background] Jesus answers with the hundredfold and the twelve thrones (19:28-29).

## Places [Background]
- Perea: 'Judea beyond the Jordan' (19:1), where this teaching continues.
- Jericho: Next stop on the road (20:29).
- Jerusalem: 'Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem' (20:18).

## Key terms
- Inclusio: A literary bookend: matching words at the start and end that frame a unit (19:3; 20:15).
- Denarius: A Roman silver coin, the normal pay for a full day's work.
- The hours: Counted from sunrise: third hour about 9 a.m., sixth noon, ninth 3 p.m., eleventh 5 p.m.
- Ayin ra'ah: Hebrew 'evil eye': stinginess, a begrudging spirit.
- Jubilee: The fiftieth year of release, when land returned and slaves went free (Leviticus 25).
- Parable: A story that surprises; the lesson is often in the surprising moment.

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Day laborers: Day laborers gathered in the marketplace to be hired (20:3) and lived hand to mouth. The Torah protected them: wages before sunset (Deuteronomy 24:15). On working hours the Mishnah says everything follows 'the regional custom in these matters' (Mishnah Bava Metzia 7:1).
- Vineyards: Harvest and pruning needed many hands at once, which helps explain repeated hiring. Vineyards had walls and watchtowers (Isaiah 5:2), and the vineyard was a standing picture of Israel.
- Jubilee: Every fiftieth year land returned to its families and Israelite slaves were released (Leviticus 25:8-17). Isaiah 61 takes up the language of release for the coming age, and Jesus reads it at Nazareth (Luke 4:18-21).

## Early witnesses [Background: sourced]
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "By a vineyard He means the injunctions of God and His commandments: by the time of laboring, the present life" Homilies on Matthew 64, on 20:1-16. Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 10 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "For that place is pure from envy and jealousy." Homilies on Matthew 64, on 20:11-15. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "to the former, that they may not be proud, neither reproach those called at the eleventh hour" Homilies on Matthew 64, on 20:1-16. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Who are the first and the last? Readings include Israel and the Gentiles, the disciples and later believers, the religious leaders and sinners, and those converted early or late in life (Chrysostom's view). The video applies it to anyone with a wage-earning mindset.
- Is the parable about salvation or rewards? Some see one gift of eternal life for all; others see a warning about comparing rewards. Both read the denarius as grace, not pay.
- Jubilee in the background? The video hears Isaiah 61 and Jubilee in the parable. Others see the main background in Israel as God's vineyard (Isaiah 5) and in Torah laws on wages.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- A denarius was a Roman coin; a drachma was a Greek coin of roughly the same value, not another name for it.
- The 10-hour workday attributed to D. A. Carson is given without a source; the Mishnah says working hours follow local custom (Bava Metzia 7:1).
- The Craig Blomberg passage on the inclusio is read from a commentary the video does not name, so this page summarizes it rather than quoting it.
- In 20:15 the LSB already has 'Is it not lawful' and 'is your eye envious,' where the video's translation reads am I not allowed and do you begrudge my generosity.
- Proverbs 23:6 reads 'a selfish man' in the LSB and 28:22 'a man with an evil eye'; the video's translation says stingy for both.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. Which worker do you identify with first, and why?
2. Why does the master pay the last first, in front of everyone?
3. What is the difference between being treated unfairly and being treated generously to someone else?
4. Where do you notice a 'bad eye' in yourself, looking for what is wrong?
5. How do marriage and wealth point outward, as vehicles of blessing?
6. Whom could you extend 'radical mercy' to this week?

## Application
- (video) The lesson, stated plainly: the real currency in the kingdom of heaven is not money, it's mercy. Those who are fit for the kingdom must have God's good eye and extend radical mercy to all who need it. In God's kingdom, true satisfaction comes from seeing everyone blessed, not just yourself. If God's people truly understood this, no one would ask whether divorce is allowed or how many deeds earn entrance. Marriage and wealth are vehicles to extend God's blessings to others. The world's influence comes in like the tide; we can't think like the world. Put on the glasses of radical generosity and you will see potential, providence and opportunities to spread the kingdom.
- Study note (added): the next time you hear of someone else's blessing, notice your first reaction. Thank God for it out loud, and pray Matthew 6:22 for a clear eye.
